sources.text:

U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday awarded the Medal of Freedom, the country’s highest civilian honor, to Rudy Giuliani, the former New York mayor who became a national figure after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks and later helped Trump try to overturn his 2020 election defeat.
Trump announced he would honor Giuliani, 82, in September 2025 shortly after the former mayor was badly injured in a car accident. Trump at the time called him “the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot.”
After the 9/11 attacks, Giuliani became one of the most popular figures in U.S. politics. He launched a Republican presidential bid in 2007, and even after it failed, he remained a prominent conservative messenger.
In a statement, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales called Giuliani “a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our nation.”
Trump awarded the medal in a private Oval Office ceremony.
Giuliani in a statement said he was “honored and humbled” by the medal, and credited advice from President Ronald Reagan, under whom he served as associate attorney general and a U.S. Attorney, for guiding his public service.
From the Archives: Rudy Giuliani found in contempt of court in $148-million defamation case
“I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me – particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together,” Giuliani said.
His son, former Trump administration official Andrew Giuliani, told reporters outside the White House that the ceremony was a “special” gathering in which Trump and Giuliani reminisced about their long friendship.
Their alliance deepened after Trump lost the 2020 election. Giuliani advanced falsehoods about the result and the integrity of the voting process. He held a press conference at a Philadelphia landscaping business, where he made claims that were widely rebutted, then another at the headquarters of the Republican National Committee where hair dye dribbled down his face.
His false claims came with legal consequences. He was barred from practicing law in New York, where he once served as the U.S. Attorney in the state’s southern district, and Washington, and faced criminal charges in Georgia and Arizona for attempting to subvert the 2020 election results.
Two Georgia election workers won a $148-million judgment against Giuliani in December 2023 for defamation. He “fully satisfied” the terms of the judgment in February 2025.
By the end of that year, Trump pardoned him for federal criminal offenses.
With Giuliani’s medal, Trump has awarded the Medal of Freedom 27 times between his two terms. He has predominantly reserved the honor – designated by President John F. Kennedy for “meritorious contribution” to U.S. security or national interests, world peace or cultural endeavors – for former athletes. Fourteen of Trump’s awards have been to retired athletes, some of whom also served in public office.
He has said he plans to award the medal to retired and scandal-plagued Major League Baseball pitcher Roger Clemens and U.S. national hockey team goaltender Connor Hellebuyck.
Trump posthumously awarded the medal to slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk in October 2025.

sources.news_title: President Trump Awards Rudy Giuliani The Presidential Medal Of Freedom – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Isaac
sources.text:
President Trump has awarded Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom, giving “America’s Mayor” the nation’s highest civilian honor in a White House ceremony Tuesday.
The honor recognizes a public career that took Giuliani from a relentless federal prosecutor to the mayor who helped lead New York City through the horror of September 11, 2001.
It also delivers a powerful answer to the years-long campaign to erase everything Giuliani accomplished simply because he stood beside President Trump when the political cost was at its highest.
The White House previewed the ceremony with a look back at Giuliani’s fight against organized crime, transformation of New York and leadership after 9/11:
From leading the fight against crime to transforming New York City & demonstrating unwavering leadership after 9/11, Rudy Giuliani has left an undeniable mark on American history.
Today, @POTUS will honor Mayor Giuliani, America’s Mayor, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom. pic.twitter.com/CNRDxm261j
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 24, 2026
CBS News reports that the Oval Office ceremony was scheduled for 11 a.m. Eastern and was closed to the press. The White House praised Giuliani as a dedicated public servant whose leadership left a lasting mark on both New York City and the country, citing his record against organized crime, his mayoral turnaround and his steadiness after 9/11.
The administration’s case for the award reaches well beyond one chapter of his life. As U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, Giuliani pursued mob bosses and made his name in the war on organized crime.
As mayor, he oversaw a dramatic crime decline and the revival of a city many people had written off.
Then came 9/11.
Giuliani became a steady national voice while smoke still hung over Lower Manhattan, emergency crews searched the ruins and families waited for news that too often never came. That leadership made the title “America’s Mayor” more than a campaign slogan.
The White House said those years of service left an undeniable mark on the country.
After receiving the medal, Giuliani shared the honor with the people who worked with him, challenged him and sacrificed alongside him:
I am honored and humbled to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom from my nation and from President Donald J. Trump.
Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: "There is no limit… pic.twitter.com/hKb7qi5Tc8
— Rudy W. Giuliani (@RudyGiuliani) November 24, 2026
Giuliani credited Ronald Reagan’s lesson that there is no limit to what a person can accomplish when he does not care who receives the credit. He specifically honored colleagues, friends and those who lost their lives in the causes they shared, then closed by thanking God and blessing the United States.
The Associated Press reports that President Trump formally presented the medal Tuesday and that Giuliani’s son, Andrew, emerged from the private ceremony visibly moved. Andrew Giuliani said the moment was difficult to put into words and described the honor of watching his father receive the award from a president who has known him for decades.
The award is the highest civilian distinction the president can bestow. It is reserved for people whose work has made an exceptional contribution to America’s security, national interests, culture, world peace or other major public and private endeavors.
President Trump first announced his intention to honor Giuliani in September 2025, shortly after the former mayor was injured in a car crash. Tuesday’s ceremony completed that promise.
The night before the presentation, Giuliani was welcomed at a dinner hosted by the Italian ambassador, with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick among those marking the occasion:
The Italian ambassador hosted a dinner for @RudyGiuliani on the eve of his Presidential Medal of freedom Ceremony. @howardlutnick holds a special bond with the mayor. (Posted by staff) pic.twitter.com/oP3a86x935
— Rudy W. Giuliani (@RudyGiuliani) November 24, 2026
There is no pretending Giuliani’s story has been easy. He took ferocious political and legal fire after defending President Trump and challenging the 2020 election.
The same media class that once celebrated his leadership after 9/11 spent years trying to reduce his entire life to its preferred political narrative.
President Trump chose to look at the whole record.
He honored the prosecutor who took on the mob, the mayor who helped rescue New York from violent decline, the leader who stood in the wreckage on America’s darkest morning and the friend who refused to abandon him when Washington demanded it.
That is a record worth remembering — and on Tuesday, the White House made sure America did.

sources.news_title: Trump finally rewards Giuliani’s dopey devotion
sources.text:
Laser-focused on what matters as always, President Donald Trump is spending the day giving his disgraced former lawyer Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Sure, why not? It’s not like there is anything else big going on right now.
But apparently this very important event will be closed to the press, robbing us all of the chance to watch two doddering, crumbling old men clinging to the last bits of life pat each other on the back yet again. Huge loss for Americans, right?
In theory, this medal will honor Giuliani’s efforts as mayor of New York following Sept. 11, but let’s face it: This is really just a consolation prize since Trump pretty much let Giuliani twist in the wind even after Rudy was one of his strongest soldiers in the fight to overturn the 2020 election.
Well, one of Trump’s strongest, weirdest soldiers.
Who can forget the ill-fated, histrionic press conference at Four Seasons Total Landscaping, for example? Or the cascade of hair dye running down Giuliani’s face at a desperate, sweaty November 2020 press conference filled with conspiracy-mongering and lies?
But Giuliani was not rewarded for his loyalty. There was no job for him in the second Trump administration. Rudy was left in the cold just like MyPillow magnate Mike Lindell, who also was not tapped as one of the many election deniers stuffed into the administration now.
Giuliani has had a rough time since 2020, and pretty much all of it traces back to his efforts to help Trump overturn the election.
He was disbarred in New York over it.
He was disbarred in Washington, D.C., over it.
He lost a defamation suit brought by two former Georgia election workers he defamed, with the court awarding Ruby Freeman and her daughter, Shaye Moss, $148 million. Giuliani spent a lot of time trying to dodge that payment, but ultimately settled up for an undisclosed amount in early 2025.
He also settled a defamation suit with Dominion Voting Systems for an undisclosed amount.
And he was ordered by a New York court to pay his former defense lawyers $1.36 million in legal fees he was stiffing them on.
Whew. That is a string of bad luck! Meanwhile, Trump has made over $2 billion since retaking office in 2025. He could pay off all of Giuliani’s debts, and it would be no more than a rounding error in his bank account.
But instead, Trump’s largesse toward Giuliani seems limited to empty gestures.
Related | Worst masterminds of Trump’s attempted coup get pardons
First, there was the meaningless pardon he coughed up for Giuliani and 76 other stalwart election deniers. These were all meaningless because none of them, Giuliani included, were facing federal charges, and Trump, much to his chagrin, can’t pardon state offenses.
And then was the big announcement that he’d be awarding Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom after Giuliani was injured in a car crash in September 2025. Trump raced to Truth Social to say Giuliani was the “greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot.”
It’s unclear why Trump felt so inspired at that particular moment. Perhaps he thought Giuliani was on death’s door. It’s also unclear why it took 14 months to get around to draping this thing around Giuliani’s neck, but apparently today is the day.
Congrats, Rudy. We’d say wear it with pride, but no one connected to Trump should ever have pride in their work.

sources.text:
A man barred from practicing law in two jurisdictions and named as an unindicted co-conspirator in a federal election interference case has now received the nation’s most prestigious civilian decoration.
President Donald Trump presented Rudy Giuliani, 82, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom during a private Oval Office ceremony on Tuesday, making him the third recipient of the award during Trump’s second term.
The honor, which has historically recognized extraordinary contributions to American public life, was framed by the White House around Giuliani’s decades of public service and his leadership in the aftermath of the September 11 terrorist attacks.
White House spokesperson Olivia Wales captured the administration’s position plainly, stating that “President Trump will proudly honor Mayor Giuliani — America’s Mayor — with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for his lifetime of service to the American people.”
Giuliani himself previewed the honor a day before the ceremony, confirming his selection during an appearance on former Trump adviser Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast, and later said he was “honored and humbled” to receive the medal.
Trump had actually announced his intention to confer the award back in September 2025, just days after Giuliani suffered serious injuries in an automobile accident in New Hampshire, framing the gesture in part as a show of loyalty to a longtime ally.
Writing on Truth Social at the time, Trump called Giuliani “the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot,” cementing what Andrew Giuliani described Tuesday as a friendship spanning four decades.
Andrew Giuliani, who leads the White House Task Force for the FIFA World Cup 2026, told reporters outside the Oval Office that Trump reflected warmly on his father’s tenure as New York City mayor, a role Rudy held from 1994 to 2001.
The award arrives despite a legal record that has shadowed Giuliani for years, including his role representing Trump in lawsuits seeking to reverse the 2020 presidential election results, which led to his disbarment in both New York and Washington D.C.
He also faced criminal charges in Georgia and Arizona related to those efforts, and special counsel Jack Smith identified him as an unindicted co-conspirator in the federal election interference case against Trump, all of which Giuliani has denied.
Trump’s support for Giuliani has been consistent throughout those legal battles, including appointing him to an advisory council within the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year.
Giuliani joins conservative activist Charlie Kirk and 9/11 hero Welles Crowther as Medal of Freedom recipients during Trump’s current term, both of whom received the honor posthumously, bringing Trump’s total presentations of the medal across both his presidencies to 26.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Tuesday awarded former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, during a private ceremony in the Oval Office.
Giuliani, 82, received the medal for his decades of public service, including his tenure as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, his two terms as mayor of New York City, and his leadership after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, when he became widely known as “America’s Mayor.”
White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said Trump was proud to honor Giuliani for “a lifetime of service to the American people.”

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is the highest civilian honor in the U.S. and recognizes an individual's contributions to the security or national interests of the United States, to world peace, or to cultural or other significant public or private endeavors. The award was established by President John F. Kennedy in 1963, expanding on an existing Medal of Freedom that honored wartime civilian service. Some legacies are forged in dust. Twenty-five years ago, a gray cloud swallowed lower Manhattan whole – steel, glass, and three thousand lives reduced to ash in a single morning. While the world watched in paralyzed horror, one man walked toward the wreckage.
In the quarter-century since, that man has been lionized, demonized, disbarred, and dragged through courtrooms from Georgia to Arizona. The establishment spent years trying to reduce him to a mugshot and a punchline – because apparently a lifetime of service to your country means nothing once you pick the wrong side of the political aisle. They bankrupted him. They stripped his law license. They wanted America to forget what he’d done when it mattered most.
America didn’t forget.
On Tuesday, President Trump will award Rudy Giuliani – “America’s Mayor” – the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in a White House ceremony before the first family departs for Thanksgiving at Mar-a-Lago. Hard to think of a more fitting way to start a holiday built around gratitude.
A lifetime of service
The medal recognizes a career that most public servants couldn’t match in three lifetimes. As the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan, Giuliani dismantled the Mafia’s stranglehold on New York. As mayor, he turned a city synonymous with crime into one of the safest in the world. And on September 11, 2001, he became the steady voice a shattered nation desperately needed. White House assistant press secretary Olivia Wales put it plainly:

As U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Mayor Giuliani took down mob bosses and led a relentless war on crime. President Donald Trump awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani on Tuesday, Nov. 24, recognizing his decades of public service, including his leadership during the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks that brought him national prominence.
The presentation took place during a private ceremony in the Oval Office attended by Giuliani’s family and close friends. The event fulfilled a promise Trump made in September 2025 to honor the 82-year-old former mayor, who later served as the president’s personal attorney and political adviser.
According to The Associated Press, the recognition places Giuliani among recipients of the nation’s highest civilian decoration, awarded to individuals who have made exceptional contributions to American national interests, public service, culture and other fields.
Giuliani’s son, Andrew, described the closed-door presentation as a meaningful occasion for the family.
Speaking with reporters outside the White House, Andrew Giuliani said, “I don’t know, but it was really a wonderful and special ceremony.”
According to The Jerusalem Post’s account of the ceremony, Trump spoke about Giuliani’s leadership as mayor and recalled their personal relationship, which began more than four decades ago, before Giuliani first took office.
Andrew Giuliani said family members and friends attended the presentation, including his wife and daughter. He described the experience as emotionally significant and expressed appreciation for the recognition.
“I’m so proud of my father. I’m so proud to be his son,” he said.
Trump announced his intention to award Giuliani the medal in September 2025, shortly after the former mayor was injured in a vehicle accident in New Hampshire.
At the time, the president praised Giuliani as the “greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot.”
The White House reiterated that position ahead of Tuesday’s ceremony, emphasizing Giuliani’s public service and his role in guiding New York City through the aftermath of the Sept. 11 attacks.
Giuliani served as mayor from 1994 through 2001, overseeing changes in the city’s policing strategies, municipal administration and public safety policies. His tenure included substantial declines in reported violent crime, although aspects of his administration’s law enforcement practices generated controversy.
Before becoming mayor, Giuliani served as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, where he gained prominence prosecuting organized crime, public corruption and financial misconduct.
His national recognition grew considerably following the Sept. 11 attacks, when terrorists hijacked four commercial aircraft and struck the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon near Washington and a field in Pennsylvania.
Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the attacks, including hundreds of firefighters, police officers and emergency responders.
As mayor, Giuliani coordinated with emergency personnel, appeared at public briefings and became a prominent figure in the city’s recovery efforts. His visibility and leadership during the crisis earned him the nickname “America’s Mayor.”
He was named Time magazine’s Person of the Year in 2001 and received widespread recognition for his role in the immediate response to the attacks.
Following his departure from City Hall, Giuliani entered consulting and national politics, eventually seeking the Republican presidential nomination in 2008.
He later became an adviser to Trump, supporting his 2016 presidential campaign and representing him during legal and political controversies.
Giuliani played a prominent role in challenging the results of the 2020 presidential election, advancing allegations of widespread voter fraud that were rejected by courts.
His involvement subsequently resulted in professional disciplinary proceedings, including disbarment in New York and Washington, D.C., over false statements concerning the election.
In 2023, a federal judge found Giuliani liable for defaming Georgia election workers Ruby Freeman and Shaye Moss. A jury subsequently awarded the women approximately $148 million in damages, leading to additional litigation and bankruptcy proceedings.
Giuliani also faced criminal charges in Georgia and Arizona connected to alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election results. He pleaded not guilty, and the cases were later dismissed.
Despite those controversies, Trump has maintained his support for Giuliani, frequently emphasizing his contributions as a federal prosecutor and New York City mayor.
During a Monday appearance on Steve Bannon’s War Room program, reported by CBS News, Giuliani expressed gratitude for the upcoming presentation.
“I’m of course very, very humbled and very honored not only to receive it, but to receive it from him,” Giuliani said.
The Presidential Medal of Freedom was established in its modern form by President John F. Kennedy in 1963, expanding an earlier civilian recognition program created during President Harry Truman’s administration.
The award recognizes individuals whose contributions have advanced national security, American interests, world peace, cultural achievement or other significant public and private endeavors.
Presidents have broad discretion in selecting recipients, and the honor does not require congressional approval.
Trump awarded the medal to 24 individuals during his first presidential term, including golfer Tiger Woods, baseball Hall of Famer Mariano Rivera, former football coach Lou Holtz and conservative radio commentator Rush Limbaugh.
During his second term, Trump previously awarded the medal posthumously to conservative activist Charlie Kirk and Welles Crowther, a former equities trader who died while helping others escape the World Trade Center during the Sept. 11 attacks.
Giuliani’s recognition marks another presentation honoring an individual closely associated with the events of September 2001.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who lost his brother and hundreds of colleagues in the attacks, praised Giuliani’s leadership ahead of Tuesday’s ceremony.
Lutnick previously led Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services company that lost 658 employees when terrorists struck the World Trade Center.
According to the New York Post, Lutnick credited Giuliani with providing leadership during one of the most difficult periods in New York City’s history.
Tuesday’s ceremony also highlighted the longstanding personal relationship between Trump and Giuliani, whose political association continued through both of Trump’s presidential campaigns and subsequent legal disputes.
The White House did not hold a public presentation or make the full remarks from the ceremony immediately available.
Nevertheless, Giuliani’s family described the occasion as an emotional recognition of his public career, particularly his leadership during the terrorist attacks that shaped his final months as mayor.
The award adds the nation’s highest civilian honor to Giuliani’s record of public service, recognizing a career that included federal law enforcement, two terms as New York City’s mayor and a prominent role in national Republican politics.

sources.text:
Trump presents Rudy Giuliani with Presidential Medal of Freedom
Washington — President Trump presented Rudy Giuliani, the former New York City mayor who served as his personal lawyer during the 2020 election, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday.
The White House praised Giuliani for his work across his career as a federal prosecutor in New York and then as mayor of New York City. The Medal of Freedom ceremony was set to take place in the Oval Office at 11 a.m. ET, according to Mr. Trump's schedule.
"Mayor Rudy Giuliani is a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said in a statement. "As U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Mayor Giuliani took down mob bosses and led a relentless war on crime. As Mayor, he transformed New York from a crime-ridden city into one of the safest big cities in the world, fostering economic opportunity and cultural greatness. And in the aftermath of the tragic September 11th attacks, he displayed strong American leadership in the face of evil."
Giuliani said he is "honored and humbled" to receive the award.
"Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: 'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn't mind who gets the credit.' I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together,'" he said in a statement. "And to my family — mother, father, children, ancestors, and extended family, including my friends — what you have done will always mean the most. Doing the right thing for others has been my guiding light."
Giuliani told conservative commentator Steve Bannon on his podcast Monday that he would be receiving the nation's highest civilian honor at the White House.
"I'm of course very, very humbled and very honored not only to receive it, but to receive it from him," he told Bannon during his "War Room" podcast and livestream.
Created in 1945 by President Harry S. Truman, the Presidential Medal of Freedom recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to the security or national interests of the U.S., world peace and cultural or other public or private endeavors.
Across his two terms, Mr. Trump has so far awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to 26 people, according to the Congressional Research Service. Giuliani will be the third person to receive the honor from Mr. Trump in his second term. The president posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to conservative activist activist Charlie Kirk last year after he was fatally shot on a college campus in Utah, as well as to Welles Crowther, a Boston College graduate who died in the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.
The president has said he plans to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Ben Carson, a former neurosurgeon who led the Department of Housing and Urban Development during Mr. Trump's first term; Connor Hellebuyck, Team USA men's hockey goalie; and Roger Clemens, former Major League Baseball pitcher.
Mr. Trump announced in September 2025 that he would be awarding Giuliani, 82, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom and said details would be forthcoming. The president hailed Giuliani as the "greatest mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot."
Mr. Trump announced that Giuliani would be honored days after the former mayor was injured in a car crash in New Hampshire and hospitalized.
Giuliani rose to prominence as mayor of New York City in the 1990s and became known as "America's mayor" for his leadership following the 9/11 terror attacks. He mounted a run for the GOP presidential nomination in 2008 but ended his campaign after placing third in the Florida primary.
He became a close friend and adviser to Mr. Trump's in his first term and worked as a personal lawyer to Mr. Trump during the 2020 presidential election, during which he spread baseless claims that the contest was rife with widespread voter fraud and stolen from Mr. Trump.
Giuliani was disbarred from practicing law in New York and the District of Columbia as a result of the false statements he made about the integrity of the 2020 election. He was also found liable by a federal judge in 2023 for defaming two former election workers in Georgia and ordered to pay them $148 million. Giuliani filed for bankruptcy following the decision.
The former mayor also faced state charges in Georgia and Arizona in criminal cases stemming from alleged efforts to overturn results of the 2020 election in both states. He pleaded not guilty, and both cases were dismissed.

In the weeks after his defeat to Joe Biden, Trump leaned on Giuliani and other members of his legal team to file legal challenges aimed at halting or reversing the certification of the election results in a number of states.
But after Trump returned to the White House last year, he issued pardons for members of his 2020 campaign legal team, including Giuliani, for their involvement in the scheme.
Giuliani’s 2024 disbarment was a stark fall from grace for the man formerly known as “America’s Mayor” for his handling of the events of 9/11. In 2001, he was named Time magazine’s Person of the Year.
Speaking to Bannon on Monday, he theorized he was receiving the award in recognition of his response to the terror attack - the 25th anniversary of which was marked this September.
“Well, I'll have to see what the citation says, but I mean, if I would just view it, I would assume it would be September 11,” he said. “I always thought of that as way beyond anything that I could handle.”
Bannon heaped praise on Giuliani during their interview, after the former mayor said he had merely copied former President Reagan in how he handled the role.
“You're humble about this, Rudy, you come across, and it's never about you, Rudy,” Bannon said. “ It's all about the mission. It's all about the country and putting the country first and putting citizens first. Rudy, you're an inspiration to many people.”
On Monday evening, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick - whose brother was one of the 658 Cantor Fitzgerald employees killed in the 9/11 attacks - celebrated Giuliani at a dinner hosted by the Italian ambassador to the U.S.
“I lost all the people who worked for me. He lost all the people who worked for him,” Lutnick said. “Our hearts were broken.”
Giuliani is set to become the third person awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom during Trump’s second term.
The previous recipients both received the award posthumously. The first is Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, who received the award in October 2025, following his assassination last year.
The second is equities trader Welles Crowther, who received the award in September this year as part of the commemoration of the 25th anniversary of 9/11. He died while rescuing people from the South Tower.
Trump has previously announced plans to award former Housing and Urban Development Secretary Ben Carson; Connor Hellebuyck, a 2026 Winter Olympics hockey gold medalist; and legendary baseball pitcher Roger Clemens.

Yet the former prosecutor — who went on to become Mr Trump’s personal attorney — has faced steep repercussions in recent years. After promoting misinformation about the 2020 election, he was ordered in 2023 to pay $148 million (€134m) in damages for defamation tied to his election fraud claims.

President Donald Trump is preparing to honor one of his most loyal allies with the nation’s highest civilian award, recognizing former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani for his decades of public service, his aggressive crackdown on organized crime, and his leadership during the devastating September 11 terrorist attacks.
Giuliani, 82, will receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom during an Oval Office ceremony Tuesday, marking a significant moment for the former federal prosecutor and Republican mayor whose career has spanned some of the most consequential events in modern American history.
The ceremony is scheduled to take place shortly before Trump and first lady Melania Trump depart Washington for Florida, where they will spend Thanksgiving at Mar-a-Lago.
For Giuliani, the recognition represents a major honor following years of legal battles, political controversy, and unwavering loyalty to the president.
“I am honored and humbled to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom from my nation and from our Commander-in-Chief, President Donald J. Trump,” Giuliani told Fox News.
The award also fulfills a promise Trump made more than a year ago, following a serious automobile accident that left the former mayor injured.
In August 2025, Giuliani was traveling through New Hampshire with spokesman Ted Goodman when the two reportedly stopped to assist a woman seeking help following a domestic violence incident.
Giuliani was subsequently injured in a vehicle collision, prompting widespread concern among his supporters.
Trump responded by publicly announcing his intention to award Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
“Details as to time and place to follow,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, describing his longtime friend as “the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot.”
Nearly 15 months later, the president is following through on that commitment.
The White House has emphasized Giuliani’s lengthy record in public service, particularly his work fighting organized crime and his leadership during one of America’s darkest moments.
White House assistant press secretary Olivia Wales highlighted Giuliani’s tenure as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan, where he built a national reputation for aggressively pursuing powerful criminal organizations.
Wales credited Giuliani with having “took down mob bosses and led a relentless war on crime” before becoming mayor of New York City.
As U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, Giuliani became known for his aggressive prosecution of organized crime figures, corrupt officials, and major financial crimes.
His efforts against New York’s powerful Mafia families helped establish his reputation as a relentless law enforcement figure willing to confront some of the country’s most notorious criminal organizations.
That reputation followed him into City Hall, where he served two terms as New York City’s mayor from 1994 until 2001.
During his administration, New York experienced a dramatic reduction in violent crime, helping transform the city’s national reputation after years of concerns about public safety.
Although criminologists continue to debate the relative impact of Giuliani’s policing policies and broader national crime trends, the city’s declining crime rate became one of the defining accomplishments associated with his mayoralty.
But it was Giuliani’s leadership following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks that elevated him from a prominent local politician into an internationally recognized figure.
When terrorists hijacked commercial aircraft and struck the World Trade Center, killing nearly 3,000 people, Giuliani became one of the most visible public officials responding to the unfolding catastrophe.
As Lower Manhattan descended into chaos, Giuliani appeared repeatedly before cameras, providing updates, coordinating with emergency officials, and attempting to reassure a frightened city.
His presence during the crisis earned him widespread recognition and the nickname “America’s Mayor.”
For millions of Americans, Giuliani became one of the defining public faces of the nation’s response to the deadliest terrorist attack on American soil.
His leadership during that period remains a central part of his public legacy, even as his later political activities have generated intense controversy.
In the years following his mayoralty, Giuliani became a close political ally and personal attorney to Donald Trump.
He played a prominent role in Trump’s efforts to challenge the results of the 2020 presidential election, a decision that ultimately brought significant legal and financial consequences.
In July 2024, Giuliani was disbarred in New York over false statements concerning the election. Washington, D.C., followed with a separate disbarment decision that September.
His legal troubles also included a high-profile defamation case brought by Georgia election workers Ruby Freeman and Shaye Moss.
In 2023, a federal jury ordered Giuliani to pay $148 million after finding him liable for defamation involving accusations he made against the two women.
Following bankruptcy proceedings, Giuliani reached a settlement with Freeman and Moss in January 2025.
Despite the enormous financial and professional consequences, Giuliani remained publicly aligned with Trump.
His legal circumstances subsequently changed as several election-related cases took new turns.
In November 2025, Trump issued pardons to Giuliani and 76 other individuals connected to efforts to challenge the 2020 presidential election results.
Those pardons applied to potential federal offenses and did not eliminate state-level allegations or civil judgments.
Weeks later, a Georgia judge dismissed the state’s election-related racketeering prosecution against Trump, Giuliani, and several other defendants after prosecutors declined to continue the case.
Giuliani has also remained connected to legal proceedings in Arizona, where Attorney General Kris Mayes indicated that prosecutors could pursue a new indictment following the dismissal of an earlier case.
Throughout the controversies, Trump has continued defending his former attorney and publicly recognizing his accomplishments.
The upcoming Medal of Freedom ceremony underscores that longstanding relationship while placing renewed attention on Giuliani’s earlier career in law enforcement and public leadership.
The Presidential Medal of Freedom is the highest civilian decoration awarded by the United States government.
Presidents have traditionally used the honor to recognize individuals who have made exceptional contributions to American society, national security, public service, culture, and other areas of national importance.
For Giuliani, the award represents recognition of a public career that began long before his association with Trump and included major roles in federal law enforcement, municipal government, and the national response to terrorism.
It also arrives at a striking moment in his personal and political life.
After years of courtroom battles, disbarment proceedings, financial difficulties, and intense public scrutiny, Giuliani is preparing to enter the Oval Office to receive one of the country’s most prestigious honors.
His critics continue to point to his conduct following the 2020 election, while supporters emphasize his record as a prosecutor, his administration’s public safety achievements, and his leadership after September 11.
Trump’s decision to award Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom makes clear which aspects of that complicated legacy the president intends to recognize.
More than two decades after Giuliani stood before a devastated New York City in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, the former mayor will be honored at the White House for his service to the country.
And for a political figure who has remained one of Trump’s most steadfast allies through years of controversy, Tuesday’s ceremony will mark a significant public recognition from the president himself.
